transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-04
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 mins
Attendees: Mark Liu (Redwood AE), Sofia Ramirez (Redwood SE), Evan Cheng (DatumSoft), Priya Patel (DatumSoft), Tom Reynolds (DatumSoft)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Weekly POC sync to review quantization runs (INT8 / FP8) done last week, discuss quality deltas on customer evals, perf numbers on A100/H100, and agree next steps for deeper benchmarking and runtime config tuning.

Topics: quantization results, eval metric deltas, perf tradeoffs, runtime fallbacks, next steps, security/PCI implications briefly.

Transcript:
[00:00] Mark Liu: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, uh, quick agenda - recap of the INT8/FP8 runs we pushed Monday, look at the eval deltas on your prompt set, and plan next week's tests. Sofia and I will own the perf runs, Evan you'll own the eval labels.
[00:18] Evan Cheng: Thanks Mark, yeah we ran the initial SKUs on H100 and A100, um, FP16 baseline then INT8 quant and the FP8 branch. We pushed results into the sheet, there's some noise in the long-form prompts.
[00:34] Sofia Ramirez: Quick note - the INT8 we used is our QAT-ish flow with per-channel scales, not naive symmetric quant; so it's slightly more conservative than the paper's toy settings. That said, throughput improved quite a bit.
[00:50] Priya Patel: When you say "improved" - can you give ballpark numbers? We need to justify to the platform team.
[01:00] Sofia Ramirez: Sure - baseline FP16 at seq=2k, batch=1 on H100 was ~12 tokens/sec p50, INT8 is ~26 tokens/sec, FP8 is ~20 tokens/sec. So roughly 2.1x for INT8 and 1.6x for FP8 on those long sequences. On A100 numbers were similar but slightly lower magnitude (INT8 ~1.9x).
[01:25] Tom Reynolds: And latency p95? We care about tail behavior more than mean.
[01:30] Sofia Ramirez: p95 did increase a touch under INT8 in the worst-case long prompts - we saw p95 go from 220ms/token to about 320ms/token at seq=2k with batch1, which suggests some kernel fallback/fragmentation under high memory pressure. FP8 p95 was 260ms/token. We're investigating kernel scheduling.
[01:50] Evan Cheng: On quality - we ran your 150 prompt sample (we'll send full 200 later) and computed rouge-L and a simple exact-match-ish metric for short-answer tasks. Delta vs FP16: INT8 average rouge-L -0.9% and EM -0.7%; FP8 average rouge-L -0.3% and EM -0.2%. So FP8 looks closer to FP16 on our set.
[02:15] Mark Liu: Good, that's inline with what we expected. One caveat - for safety-sensitive prompts we saw a couple aberrations in INT8 where hallucination risk slightly increased. Evan, can you flag examples?
[02:28] Evan Cheng: Yes - examples 23 and 47 in the sheet show changed entity names in the answer. We'll annotate those as "safety/accuracy" issues in the shared doc.
[02:38] Priya Patel: Are these deterministic or random? If they're deterministic it's easier to do rollback.
[02:43] Sofia Ramirez: Early look suggests some prompts consistently degrade under INT8; it's not just random. That's why we recommend the hybrid flow - FP8 for most gen, INT8 for less-sensitive routes, or automatic fallback to FP16 for flagged prompts.
[02:58] Tom Reynolds: Hybrid increases complexity. How much overhead to runtime do fallbacks add?
[03:03] Sofia Ramirez: Minimal if we pre-warm the FP16 path and use our prefix caching; cost is mainly extra memory headroom and small routing latency (~3-6ms) for model-switch logic. But if you have heavy concurrency, you'll need a slightly larger hosted pool or dedicated nodes.
[03:20] Mark Liu: Also keep in mind quantized models reduce GPU memory so you can host more replicas per GPU, which helps throughput/cost. We'll send a cost/replica sheet.
[03:30] Evan Cheng: On costs - preliminary cost modeling shows INT8 reduces per-token GPU spend ~40-45%, FP8 ~30-35% vs FP16. That aligns with our internal back-of-envelope.
[03:40] Priya Patel: Those numbers are attractive, but we need to validate across our 8k seq worst-case flows. Did you run 8k sequences?
[03:48] Sofia Ramirez: We did an initial 8k run but pure 8k is noisy due to memory fragmentation. For 8k, INT8 saw ~1.7x throughput improvement and some more p95 tail; FP8 was closer to 1.4x but better tail stability. We're going to run tuned kernel batches next.
[04:05] Tom Reynolds: Any compliance concerns with quantization? I know KMS/HSM is unaffected, but does model artifact change our audit surface?
[04:12] Mark Liu: Not really - model artifacts are still logged; quantized weights don't alter audit logs. For Private deployments we can show the checksum and reproducibility steps. We'll attach our security whitepaper, but nothing in SOC2/ISO requirements is violated.
[04:28] Evan Cheng: Can we get per-route rollout guidance? We have a public chatbot and an internal analytics summarizer; we might choose different profiles.
[04:36] Mark Liu: Yes - recommended plan: default FP8 for public-facing non-sensitive routes, INT8 behind an opt-in flag for internal summarization (where lower quality is tolerable), and FP16 reserved for safety-critical flows. We can provide an automated canary that routes a small percentage to FP16 when newly quantized.
[04:56] Priya Patel: About the eval rubric - what's your suggestion for thresholds? We need concrete SLOs.
[05:02] Sofia Ramirez: For rouge-L, we typically accept up to -1.5% for INT8 on generation tasks for POC, but higher sensitivity tasks (legal/medical) should be <= -0.5% delta. For short Q&A EM, we prefer <= -1% delta overall; beyond that we recommend not using INT8. These are guidelines not hard rules.
[05:20] Tom Reynolds: Sounds fair. Can you summarize the perf matrix we should expect per machine type and sequence length?
[05:26] Sofia Ramirez: We'll produce a matrix in the spreadsheet, but short summary: H100: INT8 ~2.0-2.2x (2k), 1.6-1.8x (8k); FP8 ~1.5-1.7x (2k), 1.3-1.5x (8k). A100: ~10-15% lower multiplier. p95 tail is best for FP8.
[05:45] Evan Cheng: Any known model classes where INT8 is particularly bad? Transformers with heavy elementwise ops sometimes lose fp sensitivity - transformers with very long context and position embeddings can show more drift.
[05:58] Sofia Ramirez: Right, and certain LoRA adapters can behave oddly if quantized naively - we recommended folding adapters into base weights before quant. We can help with that.
[06:08] Mark Liu: Ok let's talk actionables: Sofia will run tuned kernel tests (we mentioned) and post results; Mark will share cost breakdown; Evan will push labeled evals. Schedule wise, aim to reconvene same time next week unless we need a deep-dive earlier.
[06:22] Priya Patel: Quick question - are there any licensing or model-weights restrictions if we ship quantized models outside of Redwood?
[06:27] Mark Liu: Depends on the model license. For open models we provide quantized artifacts but check the model license; for Redwood-verified models we include redistribution notes. We'll add a note in the sheet per model.
[06:38] Tom Reynolds: Competitors - we asked Anthropic and looked at Bedrock. Any reason to pick Redwood for this flow?
[06:44] Mark Liu: Two main reasons: runtime-level fallbacks + observability (token-level error tracing), and the unified API across hosted/dedicated/private. That helps you standardize rollout.
[06:55] Evan Cheng: Ok we'll prioritize getting you the full prompt set; expect it tomorrow. We'll also flag the safety examples.
[07:02] Mark Liu: Great. Before we close, any blockers?
[07:05] Priya Patel: No blockers, timeline is tight but doable.
[07:08] Tom Reynolds: None from infra.
[07:10] Mark Liu: Perfect - we'll send the spreadsheet link and security doc after the call. Thanks everyone.
